title: Adventure Story Map
goal: Your kid turns a real place they know into the setting of an adventure story. They walk it with a storyteller's eye, draw a map of it, and write a story that happens right there, on real paths and next to real landmarks. When they're done, someone can read the story with the map in hand and follow every step of the adventure.
need: A real place your kid knows: your street, a park, the garden, a trail, a holiday spot
Paper, pencils and coloured markers for the map, and a notebook for the story

lesson.text: Stories feel real when the place is real and something is at stake. Your kid needs three things: real details from the place, a character who wants something, and a problem in the way.
lesson.before: He went to the park. It was scary. Then he went home.

model.line: Leo crept past the yellow slide at Riverside Park,
where the swing chains creaked in the wind and the air smelled like wet leaves.
He had to reach the old oak by the creek before dark.
Then, behind him, the gate clicked shut.

lesson.modelNote: 'It was scary' tells the reader how to feel. The fix gives them creaking chains, a deadline and a gate clicking shut, so they feel it on their own. That swap is the one to look for in every draft.

howTo.intro: The trap here is fixing spelling while the story is still coming out. On the walk, play what-if with them. At the desk, read for the story and save spelling for the end.

plan.what: Draw the map and plan the adventure (Steps 2 and 3).
Write the story, link it to the map and share it (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: Your kid doesn't like writing yet
troubleshoot.a: They tell the story out loud while you write it down, or draw it as comic panels with a sentence under each.
Go back to a what-if from the walk, or borrow a classic: a lost pet, a hidden treasure, a race before dark.

troubleshoot.q: They want dragons, not our street
troubleshoot.a: Let the dragon land at the actual playground. Keep the map true to the place and let anything happen on it.

steps.title: Go on a what-if walk
steps.why: Your kid picks a place they know and walks it, looking for where a story could happen.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a place they know well and walks it slowly with you. At each interesting spot, you both play 'what if': what if this drain led to a tunnel? What if someone hid something in that tree? They jot down the best what-ifs and the details around them: sounds, smells, colours, hiding spots, paths.
steps.you: Walk with them and play along. Ask storyteller questions instead of grown-up ones: where would a character hide? What would you hear here at night? Let the silly ideas come. The good ones show up after the silly ones.
ask: What's the most mysterious spot here?
If a character had to hide right now, where would they go?
steps.tip: Bring the notebook on the walk. Details written on the spot ('the gate squeaks') beat details remembered at the kitchen table.

levels.explore: Point at 5 things you notice and say your best what-if for a grown-up to write.
levels.develop: Note sights, sounds and smells at 5 spots, and a what-if for each.
levels.extend: Describe one spot twice: once as a safe, happy place and once as a creepy one. Which details change the mood?

steps.title: Draw the map
steps.why: Your kid maps the place, accurately enough to find your way with it.
steps.kid: Your kid draws the place from above: the outline, the main paths, then landmarks like buildings, trees and benches. They label everything and add a compass (N, S, E, W). Older kids add a rough scale.
steps.you: Help with direction if needed: stand somewhere together and ask what's north of you. Then ask the test question that matters: could someone find their way using this map?
ask: Are bigger things drawn bigger on your map?
Which spots on the map will matter in your story?
steps.tip: Start with the paths. Once the paths are right, everything else has somewhere to go.

levels.explore: Build the place on the floor first: string for the path, a shoe for the house, a cup for the big tree. Then trace around them on paper together.
levels.develop: Draw a detailed map with labels and a compass.
levels.extend: Pace out the longest path, measure your paper, and pick a scale that makes it fit, like 1 cm for 20 steps. Check one short path against it.

steps.title: Plan the adventure
steps.why: Your kid builds the story before writing it, and puts it on the map.
steps.kid: Your kid creates a main character (a name, an age, what they want) and decides the problem: what's in the way? Then they plan a beginning, a middle where things get harder, and an ending. They mark on the map where each big moment happens.
steps.you: Ask the questions that turn a list of events into a story: what does the character want? What goes wrong? Help them plan a problem, not just a trip from one spot to the next.
ask: What does your character want, and what's stopping them?
Where on the map does the most exciting part happen?
steps.tip: If the plan is 'they walk here, then here, then home,' ask what could go wrong at the second spot. That's usually where the story is.

levels.explore: Draw your character, then draw the problem and how it gets solved in 3 boxes.
levels.develop: Plan a character, a problem, 2 or 3 things that go wrong, and an ending. Mark 3 moments on the map.
levels.extend: Plan the ending first, then plant an early clue so the twist feels fair.

steps.title: Write the story
steps.why: Your kid writes the adventure, full of details from the walk.
steps.kid: Your kid writes the story from beginning to end, using their notes: street and park names, landmarks, the sounds and smells from the walk, and a bit of dialogue. The goal is that a reader feels like they're standing right there.
steps.you: Let them write without interrupting, and don't fix spelling yet. Afterward, give one piece of feedback: 'the chase made my heart race' or 'I want to hear more about the creek.' One thing, so it feels doable.
ask: Can the reader picture exactly where your character is standing?
Did you use a real sound or smell from the walk?
steps.tip: Keep the Riverside Park example from the start nearby. Pointing at 'senses' is easier than explaining it again.

levels.explore: Tell the story aloud while a grown-up writes it, using 3 things you noticed on the walk.
levels.develop: Write several paragraphs with a clear plot, settings from your map and at least one bit of dialogue.
levels.extend: Write the full story, then cut a quarter of it: keep every landmark and lose the words that repeat.

steps.title: Link the map, share and look back
steps.why: The story and the map come together, and a reader follows the adventure, map in hand.
steps.kid: Your kid numbers each big moment of the story on the map and adds a legend, then checks that the route makes sense (no teleporting). They fix unclear sentences and spelling, then give the story and map to someone to read together.
steps.you: Be the first reader, story in one hand, map in the other. Watch whether you can follow along. Tell them the spot where you could picture it best, add one suggestion, then ask which scene they'd read aloud first.
ask: Can someone follow your story on the map, or does your character teleport?
Did exploring the real place change how you see it?
steps.tip: The best moment is watching someone trace the route with their finger while they read.

levels.explore: Put stickers on 2 or 3 story spots and share the story with one person.
levels.develop: Number every big moment, add a legend, and share with 2 people.
levels.extend: Give the story and map to someone who's never been there and watch them follow it. Rewrite every spot where they got lost.

conclusion.headline: An ordinary place has a story in it now.
conclusion.text: Walk past one of the story spots and ask what happens there. They'll point to the exact place and tell you what the character wanted and what got in the way. That pair is the engine of every story they'll write.
conclusion.celebrate: Read back the line built from something you both noticed on the walk, and add: 'I remember that exact sound. You put me right back there.'
extensions: Record it as an audiobook, reading every scene out loud
Make a story map for a place from a trip
Write the same adventure from another character's point of view
Illustrate the key scenes at their real spots on the map
Write a sequel in the same place

signs: They point out 'story spots' on ordinary walks
Their writing starts to include names, sounds and smells from the place
Their stories have a problem, not just a list of things that happened
makeItReal: Turn it into a story walk: hand the story and map to a friend or grandparent and walk the route together while they read each scene out loud at its spot. Let your kid lead and stop the group at every numbered mark.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

photo.alt: A boy crouched on a sandy Florida trail, grinning next to a tortoise
photo.caption: Florida, where my kids' stories were set. Real life sent plenty of characters.

fromHome.text: Last year in Florida, my kids each set a story in the places around us: one in a mysterious old house in the Keys, one about baby sea turtles hatching on the beach. Once the stories were written, they recorded them as audiobooks, reading every line themselves with pictures for each scene.
